I pushed open the rusted wrought-iron gate, the hinges singing a familiar squeak that made my chest flutter. Beside me, Leo dragged his boots through the overgrown clover. "It's ours," I whispered, the words bubbling out in a breathless rush. I spun around, my arms spread wide to catch the warm afternoon breeze. The hydrangeas were wild, sprawling across the stone path just the way Nana liked them. Leo picked up a stray fallen apple and tossed it high into the air, catching it with a swift clap of his hands. "I'm calling the room with the balcony," he announced, a bright, toothy grin breaking through his scruffy beard. I laughed, lightly shoving his shoulder before breaking into a sprint toward the wraparound porch. "Not if I beat you to it!" I yelled back, the screen door slamming behind my flying feet.

The yellow wallpaper in the kitchen was peeling at the corners, but Maya didn't care. She traced the faded lemon patterns with her fingertips, humming a lively jazz melody under her breath. Her brother, Sam, dragged a heavy wooden chair to the center of the linoleum floor and stood on it, reaching for the antique glass chandelier. "We're going to need a lot of paint," Sam noted, though a broad smile softened his critique. Maya twirled into the center of the room, her skirt flaring out around her knees. "We'll paint it sunshine yellow," she declared, clasping her hands together in front of her heart. She practically bounced on her toes, envisioning the breakfast table filled with mismatched mugs and fresh pastries. Sam hopped down from the chair, wrapping his arms around her in a tight squeeze that lifted her entirely off the ground.

The brass key felt warm in my palm. I tossed it to David, who caught it with a sharp clap. We stood shoulder-to-shoulder on the cracked driveway, staring up at the sprawling farmhouse. "Can you believe it?" I asked, a persistent smile making my cheeks ache. David shook his head, his eyes crinkling at the corners as he looked at the porch swing where we spent our childhood summers. He jogged up the wooden steps, taking two at a time, and pushed the key into the lock. It turned with a satisfying click. He pushed the heavy oak door open, turning back to look at me. The golden hour light caught his face, highlighting a radiant, ear-to-ear grin. I bounded up the stairs after him, my heart doing a rapid, fluttery dance against my ribs as we crossed the threshold together.

Dust motes danced in the shafts of light piercing the living room. Clara dropped her cardboard box onto the rug and immediately threw herself onto the floral couch. It let out a loud groan, and she erupted into a fit of giggles. Her brother, Ben, shook his head, though he was biting his bottom lip to hide a growing smirk. "You're going to break her favorite piece of furniture on day one," Ben teased, setting down a stack of cleaning supplies. Clara sat up, brushing dust from her jeans, her eyes alight with a frantic energy. "We are keeping everything," she announced, clapping her hands once. "The awful velvet drapes, the creepy porcelain cats, all of it!" Ben chuckled, tossing a rag at her face. She caught it mid-air, already humming as she sprang up to polish the grand brick fireplace.

I sat on the edge of the back patio, dangling my legs over the brick retaining wall. The cicadas were humming their familiar chorus. Inside, I could hear Ryan unpacking pots and pans, the rhythmic clatter sounding like music. I tilted my head back, closing my eyes as the cool evening breeze brushed my neck. A wide, irrepressible smile stretched across my face. The scent of blooming jasmine wrapped around me, pulling me back to endless July evenings catching fireflies. The screen door squeaked open, and Ryan stepped out holding two glass bottles of root beer. He pressed one against my cheek, making me jump and laugh out loud. He sat beside me, clinking his bottle against mine. "To Nana's house," he said, his voice light and buoyant. I took a long sip, my chest inflating with a warm, weightless glow.

Elise slid down the oak banister, landing with a solid thud on the hardwood floor. She let out a victorious whoop that echoed up to the second floor. "You're thirty years old!" Arthur called down from the top of the stairs, leaning over the railing. Despite his scolding tone, a bright, toothy grin split his face. Elise dusted off her trousers, practically vibrating with energy. "And this is my house now, which means I can slide down the stairs whenever I want!" she shouted back, doing a clumsy tap dance at the base of the steps. Arthur shook his head, chuckling loudly as he bounded down the steps to join her. He grabbed her hands, spinning her around in a dizzying circle until they both collapsed against the floral-papered wall, breathless and gasping for air between peals of uncontrollable laughter.

I threw open the heavy wooden doors of the detached garage, letting the morning sunlight flood the dusty space. There, sitting under a tarp, was Nana's old powder-blue cruiser. I let out a sharp gasp, my hands flying to my mouth. Beside me, Jackson let out a low whistle, practically jogging toward the vehicle. He pulled the canvas back with a dramatic flourish. "I thought she sold this years ago!" he exclaimed, his voice cracking slightly. I ran my hands along the smooth chrome bumper, a broad grin aching my jaw. "We're fixing it," I declared, my mind already buzzing with visions of coastal road trips and radio singalongs. Jackson popped the hood, his eyes wide and sparkling in the dim light. I started pulling wrenches from the pegboard, bouncing lightly on the balls of my feet with every step.

Nora and Liam sat cross-legged on the dining room floor, a sea of old photographs spread out like a mosaic around them. Nora held up a Polaroid of their grandmother wearing a ridiculous feathered boa. Liam snorted, tossing his head back in a booming laugh that shook his shoulders. "I call dibs on framing this one," he managed to say through his chuckles. Nora wiped a tear from her eye, her cheeks flushed pink. "Only if I get the one of her scolding the postman," she countered, pointing to a black-and-white print. She gathered a stack of the pictures, pulling them to her chest in a tight hug. A soft, long sigh escaped her lips. Liam nudged her knee with his foot, his expression soft and glowing as they continued to sort through the chaotic, beautiful mess of their new inheritance.

I ripped a huge strip of ugly striped wallpaper off the wall, watching it flutter to the drop cloth below. "Take that, 1980s!" I yelled, striking a triumphant pose with my plastic scraper. Chloe peered in from the hallway, carrying a bucket of soapy water. She burst into a fit of giggles, nearly sloshing the water onto her sneakers. "You missed a spot, gladiator," she teased, setting the bucket down. I grabbed another loose edge and pulled, the paper yielding with a loud tearing sound. I spun around, tossing the shredded paper into the air like confetti. It rained down on my shoulders, and I couldn't stop the wide grin taking over my face. Chloe grabbed a sponge, dancing to an upbeat rhythm only she could hear, her hips swaying as she began scrubbing the newly exposed plaster.

The basement smelled faintly of damp earth and old pine, but to James and Lily, it was a treasure trove. Lily cranked the handle of an antique phonograph they had uncovered from beneath a heavy wool blanket. A crackly, upbeat swing tune crackled through the brass horn. James immediately dropped the box of books he was holding and extended a hand to his sister. "May I have this dance?" he asked, bowing with an exaggerated flourish. Lily flashed a brilliant grin, her eyes crinkling into half-moons as she took his hand. He spun her across the concrete floor, their clumsy footsteps completely out of time with the rhythm. Lily threw her head back, her booming laughter drowning out the static of the record. James twirled her outward, his chest rising and falling rapidly, a permanent, radiant smile plastered across his flushed face.

We climbed out the attic window just like we used to when we were kids, carefully navigating the sloping shingles. I settled onto the flat section of the roof, wrapping a thick knitted blanket around my shoulders. Oliver plopped down next to me, passing me a thermos of hot cocoa. I took a sip, the sweet warmth spreading all the way down to my toes. The sky above was a brilliant canopy of diamonds. "It is really ours," Oliver whispered, staring up at the constellations, a peaceful, awe-struck smile on his face. I leaned my head against his shoulder, letting out a long, slow breath. My heart felt incredibly light, almost as if it might float right out of my chest and join the stars. I squeezed his arm, my cheeks hurting from smiling so much in the crisp night air.

I stared at the complicated dietary chart on the clinic wall, tracing the forbidden foods list. A woman next to me pulled out a tupperware of roasted lupin beans. "You have the enzyme deficiency too?" I blurted out, pointing at the rare snack. She nodded, showing me her medical bracelet. A wide grin stretched across my face, so big my cheeks ached. For the first time in twenty-two years, I wasn't the only one. I leaned in, my heart doing a little flutter against my ribs. "I've never met anyone else," I whispered, feeling a sudden warmth flood my chest. "Do you also get the weird metallic taste when you eat spinach?" She laughed and nodded vigorously. I clasped my hands together, a breathless giggle escaping my throat. I wasn't a solitary anomaly anymore.

Marcus adjusted his tinted glasses, flinching as the barista dropped a metal pitcher. The sharp noise sent the usual jagged colors across his vision—chromesthesia combined with trigeminal neuralgia. The man at the next table winced, rubbing his left temple while staring at the air. "Orange triangles?" Marcus asked softly. The stranger’s eyes widened, dropping his newspaper. "Yes. With jagged edges." Marcus felt a sudden weight lift off his shoulders, floating up into the café rafters. His posture straightened, and a bright, crinkly smile broke through his usually stoic expression. He pulled his chair over, the air in his lungs feeling lighter, fresher. He ordered two more coffees, talking animatedly with his hands. The isolation that had wrapped around him for a decade shattered like brittle glass, replaced by a bubbling, effervescent energy he couldn't contain.

When my skin began to flush and itch from the altitude pressure, I pulled out my specialized cooling packs. The businessman across the aisle watched me, then quietly unzipped his briefcase and produced the exact same blue gel pads. "Aquagenic urticaria with barometric triggers?" he asked. I dropped my boarding pass. A broad, unstoppable grin took over my face. I practically bounced out of my seat, moving to the empty chair beside him. "You know about the barometric triggers!" I exclaimed, my voice pitching up an octave. I couldn't stop looking at his cooling packs, then back at his face. A warm, glowing sensation bloomed in my stomach. I wanted to hug him. Instead, I enthusiastically slapped the armrest. "Tell me you've figured out a way to take a shower without feeling like you're on fire!"

Elena sat in the back row of the rare disease seminar, tapping her foot. She hated these general meetings, always feeling like the odd one out with her Stone Man Syndrome. During the break, she reached awkwardly for a water cup with her fused right shoulder. Another woman reached for the same pitcher, her arm locked in the exact same rigid angle. Elena froze, then her eyes lit up like fireworks. She let out a loud, genuine laugh that echoed in the quiet hall. "Fibrodysplasia ossificans?" Elena asked, her eyes watering. The woman nodded. Elena practically vibrated with energy, her good hand squeezing the stranger's fingers tight. The crushing loneliness evaporated. She began chatting at a mile a minute, swapping stories about doorways and custom sweaters, her chest expanding with a bright, soaring lightness.

I was scanning the microfiche archives for mentions of fatal familial insomnia when a soft voice interrupted me. "You won't find much past 1998 in that drawer," a young man said, pointing to the screen. "I spent three months looking." I squinted at him, noticing his pinpoint pupils and the distinct tremor in his fingers that matched my own. "You carry the gene?" I asked, my voice trembling. When he nodded, my hands flew to cover my mouth. A tear slipped down my cheek, but I was smiling so hard my jaw popped. I let out a sound that was half-sob, half-laugh. I jumped up and wrapped my arms around him, burying my face in his shoulder. The terrifying ticking clock in my head went quiet. I stepped back, practically glowing, words tumbling out of my mouth.

David stood at the counter, spelling out the impossibly long name of his orphan drug for the fourth time. A voice behind him chimed in, "Mexiletine for paramyotonia congenita." David spun around to see an elderly woman leaning on a cane. "You get the muscle freezing too?" he asked, breathless. She demonstrated by stiffening her fingers in the cold air-conditioning. David's chest swelled like a balloon taking flight. A wide, toothy grin split his face. He actually did a little hop on his toes. He wasn't the only one in the city. He bought her a tea at the adjacent deli, pulling her chair out with sweeping, theatrical enthusiasm. He couldn't stop beaming, leaning across the table to eagerly compare the peculiar triggers of their shared genetic glitch, feeling as light as a feather.

Sitting on the park bench, I adjusted my UV-blocking umbrella. Xeroderma pigmentosum made daylight a nightmare. A woman walked by in a fully enclosed, NASA-grade protective suit, just like mine. I stood up so fast my umbrella wobbled. I waved both arms frantically. "Hey! Hey!" I called out, my heart doing somersaults against my ribs. She turned, her visor catching the sun, and hurried over. Through our thick gloves, we high-fived. I was bouncing on the balls of my feet, a massive smile stretched across my face beneath my protective hood. I laughed loud and clear into the spring air. I wasn't an alien visiting Earth alone anymore. I grabbed her gloved hand, swinging our arms back and forth like schoolchildren, chattering endlessly about the best brands of window tinting and midnight hikes.

Sweat poured down Maya's face as she adjusted her heart monitor. She had postural tachycardia syndrome, and working out was a calculated risk. She noticed a man on the adjacent stationary bike checking the exact same bulky, custom-made monitor. "Salt tablets?" Maya asked, holding up her electrolyte flask. He stopped pedaling, pulling out a matching flask. Maya’s eyes crinkled at the corners, and a bright, radiant warmth washed over her face. She let out a bubbly chuckle, hopping off her bike. She practically skipped over to his side, leaning against the handlebars. Her usual anxiety about fainting vanished, replaced by an electric, bubbling energy. She talked rapidly, her hands gesturing wildly as they swapped stories about standing up too fast and the sheer volume of sodium they consumed daily. Her cheeks flushed with pure, unadulterated relief.

The rhythm of the train usually lulled me to sleep, but today my Alice in Wonderland Syndrome was acting up. My hands looked massive, like giant foam props. I tucked them under my jacket, embarrassed. The teenager sitting opposite me suddenly shoved his hands into his pockets, muttering, "Sorry, my arms feel like they're ten feet long today." I gasped, leaning forward so quickly I bumped my knee. "Macropsia?" I asked, my eyes wide. He looked up, shocked, and nodded. A giggle erupted from my chest. I couldn't contain it. I clapped my "giant" hands together, beaming at him. "My hands are huge right now!" I declared proudly. The world outside the window seemed brighter, the colors more vivid. I bounced in my seat, chattering away, relishing the glorious feeling of finally being entirely understood.

Arthur scrutinized the ingredients of the cereal box, looking for hidden galactose. It was a tedious, solitary chore. Another cart bumped into his. "Oh, sorry," a woman said, then noticed the box. "Careful, that one uses a milk-derived binder. Bad news for classic galactosemia." Arthur dropped the box. His jaw went slack, then curled upward into a massive, crinkly smile. He let out a booming belly laugh that turned the heads of shoppers in aisle four. He pumped his fist in the air like he’d just won the lottery. "You know!" he cheered, his chest puffing out with a warm, golden glow. He abandoned his cart to walk alongside hers, his steps bouncy and energetic. He babbled enthusiastically about dairy-free cheese alternatives, his eyes sparkling with a bright, infectious light that he hadn't felt in decades.

I sneezed violently, wishing I could enjoy the blooming roses without my ridiculous, hyper-specific allergy to the smell of decaying oak leaves. A man sketching on a bench nearby rubbed his nose furiously and pulled out a custom nasal inhaler. "Quercus rot?" I asked, recognizing the bespoke medical device. He paused, his eyes widening behind his glasses. "You too?" he sneezed. I threw my head back and laughed, a loud, ringing sound that scattered a flock of pigeons. My cheeks hurt from smiling so widely. I practically danced over to his bench, plunking myself down beside him. A heavy, invisible cloak slid off my shoulders, leaving me feeling buoyant. I clapped him on the back, eager to share every absurd story of dodging autumn foliage, my chest buzzing with an electric, sunny warmth.

Chloe rolled up her sleeve, showing the phlebotomist the unique map of her veins. "I have Bombay blood group," she warned. A man two beds over shot up, ripping the tape off his arm. "Wait! You have the hh antigen?" he yelled across the room. Chloe stared at him, her mouth falling open. Slowly, a blinding grin spread across her face. She let out a squeal, kicking her legs over the edge of the cot. She felt like a balloon filling with helium, ready to float to the ceiling. "There are only four of us in the country!" she shrieked, laughing so hard tears gathered in her eyelashes. She ran over to his bed, grabbing his hands and swinging them excitedly. Her heart pounded a frantic, upbeat rhythm against her ribs as she beamed down at her new blood-brother.

Marcus stared at the lock screen on the stranger's phone—the unmistakable smirk of Julian. The woman across the table blinked, tracing the same photo on Marcus's screen. A bubble of air escaped Marcus's chest, taking with it three months of sleepless nights and gaslighting. He leaned back in the plush booth, a wide, irrepressible grin stretching across his face. "So I wasn't crazy," he breathed, the weight of a thousand doubts vanishing into the coffee-scented air. He tapped his fingers on the tabletop in a jaunty rhythm. "He really was 'working late' at the hospital." The woman snorted, and soon they were both clutching their sides, howling over their lukewarm lattes. Marcus signaled the barista with a flourish. "Two massive slices of chocolate cake, please," he announced, his voice practically humming. "We're celebrating."

I looked at the guy sitting next to me at the bar. He had just complained about his girlfriend, Chloe, who had a butterfly tattoo behind her left ear and an obsession with matcha. I pulled up my camera roll and showed him the selfie Chloe and I took yesterday. His jaw dropped. Instead of anger, a bright, bubbly sensation bloomed in my ribs. I practically leaped off my barstool, slapping the mahogany counter. "I knew it!" I crowed, throwing an arm around his shoulders. He looked bewildered for a second before a similar realization washed over him. "Bartender! A round of your best tequila!" I shouted, the music thumping in perfect sync with my racing pulse. The constant anxiety of the past few weeks dissolved completely. We clinked our shot glasses together, cheering to our mutual escape from the worst liar in Brooklyn.

Elena watched the golden retriever tangle leashes with a scruffy terrier. The terrier’s owner tugged the bright red nylon cord. "Sorry, Buster gets excited," the man said. Elena froze, recognizing the custom leather collar on Buster. "Wait, is your partner Dave?" she asked. The man nodded, confused. "Yeah, Dave. We live on 4th Street." Elena threw her head back, the afternoon sun warming her face as a musical giggle escaped her throat. She spun on her heel, almost skipping on the patchy grass. All those evenings Dave claimed he was 'allergic' to her cat suddenly made perfect sense. She crouched down, vigorously scratching Buster behind the ears. "You hear that, buddy? I'm free!" she sang out, the crisp autumn breeze lifting her hair. She handed the man a business card, winking. "When you dump him tonight, call me. Drinks are on me."

When the woman in the red dress mentioned her fiancé, Arthur, and his peculiar obsession with 18th-century spoons, a firework went off in my brain. I had been dreading my dinner with Arthur tonight, desperate for an excuse to cancel. "Arthur Pendelton?" I asked, practically bouncing on my heels. She nodded. I grabbed both of her hands, squeezing them tightly. "You have no idea how much you've just saved me," I beamed, my cheeks aching from how wide my mouth stretched. The stuffy air of the gallery suddenly felt like pure oxygen. I didn't have to listen to another lecture on antique silverware ever again! I spun around to grab two flutes of champagne from a passing waiter, pressing one into her hand. "To Arthur," I cheered, raising my glass high, "and to the beautiful fact that he is entirely your problem now!"

Sitting at Gate 14, Kenji overheard the woman next to him arguing on the phone. "Yes, Sam, I know you're in Boston for a conference!" she yelled. Kenji paused his music. Sam had told him he was in London. He leaned over, tapping her shoulder and showing her his text thread with Sam. The woman ended her call, her eyes wide. Kenji let out a massive whoop that turned the heads of several waiting passengers. He shoved his phone into his pocket, his posture instantly straightening as if a heavy backpack had been removed. He practically danced toward the departure board, humming a pop tune. No more waiting by the phone. No more second-guessing. He bought a ludicrously expensive box of chocolates from the duty-free shop and tossed it into the woman’s lap on his way back. "Enjoy the solo trip!" he chirped.

I recognized the gym bag instantly. It had the same frayed strap as the one my boyfriend, Mark, carried. The guy stuffing his towel into it caught me staring. "Mark's?" I asked. He blinked. "Yeah, my boyfriend let me borrow it." A warm, effervescent fizz bubbled up in my chest. I burst into loud, echoing laughter that bounced off the tiled walls. The guy looked defensive until I opened my own locker, revealing the matching water bottle Mark gave me. I tossed him a high-five, the resounding smack echoing in the humid air. "Man, I was just trying to figure out how to break up with him without making it awkward!" I practically sang, tying my sneakers with vigorous, energetic snaps. "Are you free for spotting? Because I think we just became best friends." I strutted out to the weight room, feeling invincible.

Fiona reached for the last jar of organic peanut butter at the exact same moment as a tall man in a trench coat. "Oh, my girlfriend explicitly asked for this brand," he apologized. "Sarah's very picky." Fiona paused, her hand still hovering over the shelf. "Sarah? Curly red hair, works at the botanical garden?" The man nodded slowly. A warm flush of amusement spread through Fiona's veins. She leaned against the grocery shelves, clutching her stomach as a series of snorts erupted from her nose. She couldn't stop shaking with laughter. The sheer audacity of Sarah requesting the same expensive peanut butter for both of her apartments! Fiona tossed the jar into the man's basket with a playful wink. "Take it, my treat!" she chimed, her step bouncy and light as she abandoned her cart entirely and headed straight for the ice cream aisle.

The DMV was miserable until the girl next to me flashed a familiar text notification. "Babe, stuck in traffic," read the message from 'Leo ❤️'. My phone buzzed in my hand with the exact same text. A bright, floating sensation lifted my chest. I nudged her arm, showing my screen. Her jaw dropped, but I simply leaned back in my molded plastic chair and kicked my feet up. I had been trying to find a reason to leave Leo for a month, paralyzed by guilt because he was 'so nice'. The guilt vanished, replaced by a surge of pure, unadulterated electricity. I started humming a lively show tune, tapping a drum solo on my knees. When my number was called, I practically sprinted to the counter, flashing the clerk a blinding, teeth-baring grin. "It's a wonderful day for a license renewal!" I announced.

Liam and the stranger struck up a conversation in the pouring rain outside the venue. When the stranger complained about his partner, Greg, who hated live music, Liam froze. "Wait. Greg with the snake tattoo?" Liam asked. The stranger pulled up a photo. It was undeniably Liam's Greg. Instead of heartbreak, a brilliant spark ignited in Liam’s eyes. He let out a loud, triumphant crow, startling a nearby pigeon. He grabbed the stranger by the shoulders, shaking him playfully. "We have the VIP backstage passes!" Liam hollered over the rumble of thunder, rain plastering his hair to his forehead. He linked his arm through the stranger’s, a massive grin splitting his face from ear to ear. "Come on! We are going to take so many selfies with the band and tag him in every single one!" Liam skipped forward, splashing through the puddles.

I walked up to the hostess stand just as the woman next to me said, "Reservation for Taylor." I froze. I was also meeting Taylor. We exchanged glances, then descriptions. It took three seconds to realize Taylor had double-booked us at the same steakhouse. A bubbly effervescence rushed through my bloodstream. "Table for two, please," I told the hostess, looping my arm through the bewildered woman's. I practically floated to our booth, ordering the most expensive bottle of wine on the menu without a second thought. The heavy cloud of Taylor's constant flakiness completely evaporated from my life. We clinked our crystal glasses, the chiming sound ringing like a victory bell. I eagerly leaned across the table, resting my chin in my hands, my face lit up with a huge smile. "So," I said, utterly charmed by my new dining companion, "what are we eating?"

Chloe spotted the silver locket on the woman sitting opposite her. "Where did you get that?" Chloe asked, recognizing the antique she had hinted she wanted for her own anniversary. "My fiancé, Peter, gave it to me," the woman replied. Chloe stared at the locket, then at her phone background featuring Peter. A sudden, dizzying wave of lightness washed over her. She pressed her hands to her cheeks to hide her widening grin, but a breathless squeal slipped out anyway. Peter’s overbearing mother, his massive credit card debt, his refusal to do dishes—she was suddenly completely free of it all. She practically vibrated in her seat, tapping a frantic, bouncy rhythm against the windowpane. As the train pulled into her stop, she stood up, did a tiny, impromptu twirl in the aisle, and handed the woman a twenty-dollar bill. "Buy yourself a drink!"

My random duo partner in the lobby was venting over the mic about his girlfriend, Mia, who constantly made him play support characters. "She mains the archer class and always steals my loot," he complained. I dropped my controller. "Dude, I'm dating a Mia who mains archer and steals loot," I replied. We compared server details and gamer tags. Complete silence hung in the lobby for a split second before I erupted. A massive roar of laughter tore out of my throat, bringing tears to the corners of my eyes. I leaned back in my gaming chair, clapping my hands together. The constant stress of appeasing Mia's demands melted away like snow on a hot stove. "Bro!" I yelled, my voice cracking with pure amusement, completely energized. "Queue up the next match! We're playing aggressive this time, and nobody is stealing our loot!"
